To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

1) productive vocabulary training, where learners vocalize words, is more effective than receptive training, where learners only recognize words, and 2) scaffolding can help learners overcome the difficulties they encounter when they do not know the word they want to use, and can be a useful tool to help learners learn to ""unpack"" their own linguistic knowledge.

1) productive training is superior to receptive training in learning to read, 2) scaffolding can be useful for helping children learn to read, and 3) speech recognition is a promising technology to help children learn to read in developing countries.

(i) speech recognition-supported games can help improve literacy in developing countries; (ii) productive vocabulary training (i.e., vocalizing words) helps more than receptive vocabulary training (i..e, silent word recognition) and (iii) scaffolding hints can help learners unpack factors in their knowledge that may impact learning.
In summary, our research is concerned with
improving learning in the developing world by leveraging HCI techniques and technologies, in this case speech recognition, to help children learn to read in their second language.
the design of speech-enabled mobile applications to improve the literacy skills of children in developing countries.
the use of speech recognition to improve literacy skills in a developing world context.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the speech recognition-enabled games are a promising approach for helping rural children in developing countries learn to read, especially when they are supported by the right scaffolding.
speech recognition-enabled mobile learning games can help children in rural India improve word reading skills, but only when they are used in conjunction with productive training.
we need to do more research in HCI to understand the role of speech recognition in language learning, and the role of mobile games in language learning.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
HCI can make a positive impact on literacy in developing countries by designing speech recognition-enabled mobile applications that support productive training.
HCI research in the developing world can be used to inform the development of educational games for literacy, and vice versa.

speech recognition-supported games are a promising approach for supporting reading in a second or foreign language, but that more work needs to be done to understand how to design effective speech recognition systems for this purpose.
The main takeaway from our work is that
HCI can play a role in the design of speech recognition-enabled mobile learning applications for low-income populations.
speech recognition support in mobile applications is not only possible, but can be a useful and effective tool for improving reading skills.
the design of educational software should take into account the learner's linguistic and cognitive development, as well as the learner's cultural and social context, to better support learning.
